extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Rabelais, Renaissance satire, and classical literary instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive and stylistic guidance embedded in Rabelais' narrative—advice about language, education, and scholarly cultivation as presented in Gargantua and Pantagruel. Useful for studying Renaissance attitudes toward learning and plain speech in satirical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plain/common language
rubrics_metrics.description: “it becometh us to speak according to the common language; and that we should, as said Octavian Augustus, strive to shun all strange and unknown terms with as much heedfulness and circumspection as pilots of ships use to avoid the rocks and banks in the sea.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text condemns affected, artificially learned speech (illustrated by the Limousin who 'counterfeit[s] the French language'), showing that such affectation is mocked and punished in the narrative. Anti-pattern: flaying the Latin / using diabolical orifice of obscure coinages; positive pattern: speaking 'naturally' and in the common vernacular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise classical languages in education
rubrics_metrics.description: “I intend, and will have it so, that thou learn the languages perfectly; first of all the Greek, as Quintilian will have it; secondly, the Latin; and then the Hebrew, for the Holy Scripture sake; and then the Chaldee and Arabic likewise,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages are ranked and mandated: Greek first, then Latin, then Hebrew, then Chaldee and Arabic. This prescribes a curriculum order for a thoroughly learned scholar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate classical authors for stylistic formation
rubrics_metrics.description: “frame thy style in Greek in imitation of Plato, and for the Latin after Cicero.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic models are explicit: emulate Plato for Greek prose and Cicero for Latin. This is guidance on how to form an exemplary learned style rather than inventing new rhetorical fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know histories and cosmography by heart
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let there be no history which thou shalt not have ready in thy memory; unto the prosecuting of which design, books of cosmography will be very conducible and help thee much.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorization of histories and familiarity with cosmography are presented as measures of erudition—having histories 'ready in thy memory' is emphasized as a mark of scholarly completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the liberal arts and practical astronomy (but reject judicial astrology)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of the liberal arts of geometry, arithmetic, and music, I gave thee some taste ... Proceed further in them, and learn the remainder if thou canst. As for astronomy, study all the rules thereof. Let pass, nevertheless, the divining and judicial astrology, and the art of Lullius, as being nothing else but plain abuses and vanities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the mathematical liberal arts and the scientific rules of astronomy, but explicitly reject superstitious or predictive branches (judicial astrology and the art of Lullius). The division between legitimate scientific learning and vain/divinatory practices is drawn clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive study of natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: “in matter of the knowledge of the works of nature, I would have thee to study that exactly, and that so there be no sea, river, nor fountain, of which thou dost not know the fishes; all the fowls of the air; all the several kinds of shrubs and trees ... all the sorts of herbs and flowers ... all the various metals ... together with all the diversity of precious stones ... Let nothing of all these be hidden from thee.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exhaustive, almost encyclopaedic survey of flora, fauna, minerals and precious stones is prescribed—practical natural history knowledge is a core part of a complete education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study medicine, diverse medical authorities, and anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Then fail not most carefully to peruse the books of the Greek, Arabian, and Latin physicians, not despising the Talmudists and Cabalists; and by frequent anatomies get thee the perfect knowledge of the other world, called the microcosm, which is man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical learning should be wide-ranging (Greek, Arabic, Latin sources; even Talmudic/Cabalistic material not to be despised) and practised empirically via frequent anatomical study (dissection) to know the human microcosm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be thoroughly polished before public appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nor must any adventure henceforward to come in public, or present himself in company, that hath not been pretty well polished in the shop of Minerva.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public presentation, reputation, and social success require substantive polishing—extensive learning and cultivation are prerequisites for appearing in public or in company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve eyesight; avoid overwork that harms the eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: “For breaking his head with over-much study, he had an especial care not to do it in any case, for fear of spoiling his eyes. Which he the rather observed, for that it was told him by one of his teachers ... that the pain of the eyes was the most hurtful thing of any to the sight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pragmatic health-related caution within the educational program: do not overwork the eyes; excessive studying that endangers eyesight is to be avoided. Implied balance between study and bodily well-being.
